commenti.body:
There are broadly two types of character stories in film:

1. Character interacts with world; world changes character

2. World interacts with character; character changes world


The first category is the most prolific in stories, because I think it more closely mimics our journey through life. We meet people and circumstances that leave an impact on us, from childhood to adulthood. There's [the seven basic plots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seven_Basic_Plots) as influenced by Jung, which is a pretty good outline of these types of stories.

Much less common are the second category of stories, but you can see classic films like Forrest Gump, 12 Angry Men, Ferris Bueller's Day Off, where the basic gist of the story is that the inherent goodness of the main character interfaces with the world around him and changes it for the better.

Saltburn is like a cynical take on that, where he burns down the world around him and takes what they have. It's the fact that his character is a facade for nearly the whole film that makes it different to say Forrest Gump, but instead it becomes more like The Usual Suspects or Gone Girl, where there is a reveal that inverts what we think we know about the main character and therefore their influence upon the world around them.

Thanks for this, these are good parallels to draw. Thinking about it this morning, the audience is a kind of character in a film too, and we were led on a journey -- not merely tricked but made to realise we'd been naive in how we interpreted what the camera showed. I think having our charitable view of the main character systematically dismantled, along with some of our belief in the innocence of youth, gives some of the same psychological satisfaction of seeing a screen character change.

That’s a brilliant analysis

killing of the sacred dear (also with keoghan) was also the latter (perverted/evil version)
